parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a field of force.

markscheme_points.text: region (of space) where a force is experienced by a particle

hints: Hint 1: Think about the space around a mass or a charge even when no second object is there - what is different about that space?
parts.proper_answer: A region of space where a particle experiences a force.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a Field Means**
Think of a field as an invisible influence filling the space around something like a mass or a charge. You cannot see it, but it is there waiting to push or pull on the right kind of particle if one arrives.

Step 2: **Link to Force**
So a field of force means that any suitable particle placed at a point in that region will experience a force due to the field, without needing contact.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: State the type of field, or fields, that will give rise to a force acting on

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Ask yourself which property the particle has that a field can grab onto - it has mass but no charge, so which fields need charge to act?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Check Mass and Charge**
The particle is uncharged but it must still have mass. Electric force needs charge $q$, and magnetic force needs moving charge $qv$. Neither can act here.

Step 2: **Only Gravity Remains**
Gravitational force acts on mass, whether charged or not and whether moving or not. So only a gravitational field gives a force.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: The particle now has both mass and charge, but it is stationary - which field force requires motion as well as charge?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Stationary Charge Test**
A stationary charge still has mass, so gravity acts. It also has charge, so an electric field gives a force $F = qE$ even when $v = 0$.

Step 2: **Why No Magnetic Force**
Magnetic force is $F = Bqv\sin\theta$. With $v = 0$, this is zero. So magnetic field gives no force here.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: a charged particle moving at an angle to the field or fields.
hints: Hint 1: Now the particle has mass, has charge, and is moving across the field - think about whether any of the three field forces is now switched off.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **All Conditions Met**
Mass is present so gravitational force acts. Charge is present so electric force acts. Charge is moving at an angle to the field so there is a component of velocity perpendicular to a magnetic field, so magnetic force $Bqv\sin\theta$ is also non-zero.

Step 2: **Combine**
Therefore all three types of field can exert a force on this particle.

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem:
An electron, mass $m$ and charge $-q$, is moving at speed $v$ in a vacuum. It enters a region of uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$, as shown in Fig. 7.1.
{{figure:figure_7_1}}
Fig. 7.1
Initially, the electron is moving at right-angles to the direction of the magnetic field.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: Explain why the path of the electron in the magnetic field is the arc of a circle.

markscheme_points.text: force (always) normal to direction of motion
(magnitude of) force constant or speed is constant/kinetic energy is constant
magnetic force provides/is the centripetal force

hints: Hint 1: Recall the direction rule for magnetic force on a moving charge - how is the force direction related to the velocity direction at every instant?
Hint 2: If a force always acts at 90 degrees to motion, what does that tell you about the work done and the speed or kinetic energy?
Hint 3: What name do we give to a constant-magnitude force that always points toward the centre and bends motion into a circle?
parts.proper_answer: Magnetic force is always normal to velocity, so no work is done and speed stays constant. Magnitude $Bqv$ is constant, acting as the centripetal force, giving circular motion.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Force Always Sideways**
For a charge moving at right-angles to a uniform $B$ field, the magnetic force $F = Bqv$ always acts perpendicular to the velocity. As the direction of $v$ turns, the direction of $F$ turns with it, staying at 90 degrees.

Step 2: **Speed Stays Constant**
A force perpendicular to displacement does no work. So kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and speed $v$ do not change. Since $B$, $q$ and $v$ are all constant, the magnitude of the force $$F = Bqv$$ stays constant.

Step 3: **Centripetal Condition**
A constant-speed motion with a constant-magnitude force always directed toward the centre is exactly uniform circular motion. Here the magnetic force provides the centripetal force, so the path is an arc of a circle of constant radius.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Derive an expression, in terms of the radius $r$ of the path, for the linear momentum of the electron. Show your working.
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking of the two ways to write the force on the electron - one from circular motion and one from the magnetic field.
Hint 2: Equate those two force expressions and then isolate the combination $mv$ which is the linear momentum.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Equate the Forces**
Circular motion needs a centripetal force: $$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$ This must be supplied by the magnetic force on a charge moving normal to the field: $$F_B = Bqv$$ So: $$\frac{mv^2}{r} = Bqv$$

Step 2: **Isolate Momentum**
Cancel one $v$ from both sides: $$\frac{mv}{r} = Bq$$ Multiply by $r$: $$mv = Bqr$$ But linear momentum is $p = mv$, so: $$p = Bqr$$
